Not TV or radio, no… I don’t sit there thinking the news anchor is talking to me or anything like that.

My thoughts feel like my own, even when I’m going over things too much.\n\nDoctor: Has there been any moment when you were completely certain your colleague was not altering the files?\n\nPatient: Completely certain? I’ve seen enough of the project files to know something was being set up to put the blame on me.\n\nSorry, I’m circling. But no, I’ve never been completely certain he wasn’t altering them.\n\nDoctor: Have other people told you that your speech or thinking has become hard to follow or seems disorganized?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure. My sister once said I explain things like I’m footnoting myself, which I suppose I do.\n\nBut hard to follow? Maybe when I’m trying to explain the file issue, because there are a lot of pieces. I don’t think people mean my thinking is disorganized, more that they don’t have the background to follow the chain.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe it is possible that you might be mistaken about your colleague altering the files?\n\nPatient: I suppose anything is “possible,” in the way that, you know, a translator can misread a sentence if the context is wrong. A misplaced punctuation mark, a strange timestamp, a segment that doesn’t match the source properly—translators get trained to see that. My wife says I can spot a typo from across the room but forget where I put my keys, which is probably fair.\n\nBut actual things that no one else can see… no, I haven’t noticed anything like that.\n\nDoctor: Have you had a strong sense that there is a special message meant specifically for you in things like TV, radio, newspapers, or online posts?\n\nPatient: Not TV or radio, no… I don’t sit there thinking the news anchor is talking to me or anything like that.\n\nOnline posts can be tricky, though, because work is online now—shared files, comments, version histories, all of that.
